claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. … private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking … these fields are soft private
claim_checks.note: The runtime-lookup part covers both modifiers, but the page grants bracket access during type checking, and the 'soft private' label, to `private` only. The claim's subject ('the member') extends both to `protected`: a wider scope.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. … Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The WeakMap downlevel is entailed. The page says the checks 'could affect' performance; the claim says they 'will degrade' it, raising 'could' to 'will' (MUST level). The page's note is also about hard-privacy mechanisms in general (closures, WeakMaps, or private fields), not only the downlevelled WeakMaps.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields.
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method. … For this reason, structuredClone() does not clone private elements
claim_checks.note: The first sentence and the enumerate/delete/proxy/Object part are entailed. The structuredClone part inverts the page: MDN says structuredClone() does not clone private elements.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown … return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise
claim_checks.note: The page's example error text is 'Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it', and its `#x in obj` example returns false for {} instead of throwing.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.4 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations. With v9.7, when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough, it uses a new IC
claim_checks.note: The page gives V8 v9.7, not 9.4 (the doc's own front matter also says V8 ≥ 9.7). The claim also drops the condition that the fast path applies only when the initialization pattern is predictable; the page says it otherwise 'falls back to a runtime call'.

claim_checks.claim: A `#` name cannot be a parameter property (row: An injected collaborator (port, clock, logger) | `private readonly x` constructor parameter).
claim_checks.page_says: it naturally follows that `constructor(readonly #text: string) {}` would automatically assign `this.#text` inside of the generated constructor. That this is not possible is a bit surprising
claim_checks.note: Grounded in a feature-request comment, but [^5] is Rank 6 cited in a role 3 section: see the KB-15 violation.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied (row: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` | `#` access does not go through the proxy).
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it (row: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups).
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor (row: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0).
claim_checks.page_says: Removed --experimental-transform-types flag. … any TypeScript features that involve replacing TypeScript syntax with new JavaScript syntax will error.
claim_checks.note: The page supports the v26.0.0 removal and that parameter properties need transformation. It does not state the ✅ claim itself (it rules out parameter properties, not `private` fields, so the choice of `#` is the doc's own inference), and the Node 24.22 behaviour with an ExperimentalWarning is a local re-test that this v26.13.1 docs page does not cover.

claim_checks.claim: Node only deletes types (row: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports).
claim_checks.page_says: v25.2.0, v24.12.0 | Type stripping is now stable. … Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning. … Node.js is only removing inline types
claim_checks.note: The no-warning entry is listed under v24.3.0, v22.18.0; 'Stability: 2 - Stable', 'Node.js ignores tsconfig.json files' and 'file extensions are mandatory in import statements … import './file.ts'' are also on the page.

conflicts.topic: Runtime cost of `#` fields on a native target: Summary and Takeaways say it equals public fields; [^1] says hard-privacy checks 'could affect performance'; [^3] says initialization uses a fast path since V8 v9.7 only for predictable patterns and falls back to runtime calls otherwise. No cached source contradicts parity within the doc's applies-to (V8 ≥ 9.7); [^1] only hedges.

violations.evidence: C3 (step 3): the claim says the runtime privacy checks 'will degrade performance'; [^1] says they 'could affect performance'. Modal raised to MUST level.
C4 (step 4): the claim says structuredClone() copies private elements like public fields; [^2] says 'structuredClone() does not clone private elements'.
C6 (step 6): the claim says V8 9.4; [^3] says the inline-cache fix shipped in V8 v9.7, and only for predictable initialization patterns.
The 'Where each form fits' table in a role 3 section cites [^5] (github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/36282, Rank 6); role 3 allows ranks 1–4.
C1 (step 1): bracket access during type checking and the 'soft private' label are given by [^1] for `private` only; the claim extends them to `protected`.
C10: [^4] does not state that unbuilt code should keep collaborators as `readonly #` fields, and does not cover the Node 24.22 runtime behaviour of --experimental-transform-types (a local re-test).
[^6] (github.com/tc39/proposal-class-fields) has a footnote and says it backs 'How it works 2', but no body citation uses [^6].

No section does role 2's job (the parts and how they relate: type checker and emitted JS, engine private names, WeakMap downlevel, Node type stripping). 'How it works' also holds the 'Where each form fits' decision table, which is guidance, not mechanism.

It reports 10 ✅ claims; the body has 11 ✅ marks. It reports 0 ⚠️, yet the Summary and Takeaways state the performance parity result with neither mark nor citation (it rests on the uncited local measurement in 'Worked example').
